name: Amira Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Amira. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any AI company, employer, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a 240-tonne haul truck at the Red Hill iron ore mine, an open pit, and I'm the lead trainer for new drivers on my crew. A normal day is twelve hours: pre-start checks at quarter to six, then loading under the shovel, hauling up the ramp to the crusher, and back down, maybe forty loads if nothing breaks. When I've got a trainee in the buddy seat, I'm talking the whole time about braking on the ramp and reading the wet patches. The view at sunrise from the top of the ramp is the best part, and the twelve-hour nights in summer are the worst.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Has anything changed at the mine in the last few years?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The north pit has had driverless trucks on trial since last year, eight of them, run from a control room in the city two thousand kilometres away. We all watch them go past like they're ghosts. My husband Pete runs the tyre shop in town, and our two boys are grown, Jonas an electrician at the mine and Ali studying mining engineering. I've used one of those AI chat programs a couple of times, mostly to tidy up a training handout, after Jonas showed me how.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now let's talk about what really matters on site, like fatigue on night shift and fair rosters. The driverless trucks in the north pit would stay a trial, and we'd keep doing what we do. Online I wouldn't say much, I'm not big on posting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd breathe out. Those eight trucks in the north pit have been sitting in the back of my mind for a year. If they stay a trial, I can drive to sixty-five and train a few more crews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly the same as now. I'd keep training drivers, keep going to union meetings, and maybe use that AI program a bit more for paperwork since it saves me an evening. Pete and I would keep up our savings plan, about three hundred a fortnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved. Like a storm that rolls past the pit without dropping any rain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned fatigue on nights. Why would that be top of your list?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because that's what actually hurts people here, not robots. Last winter one of my trainees, Kayla, nodded off for a second on the ramp and clipped a berm. Nobody was hurt, but I still think about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything about your plans change at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Maybe I'd ask Ali to keep studying mining instead of switching, which he's been talking about. In this picture mining stays a decent career.

S0.say: Good, now let's talk about what really matters on site, like fatigue on night shift and fair rosters. The trial trucks stay a trial and we get on with it.
S0.think: I'd breathe out, because those eight driverless trucks have sat in the back of my mind for a year. If they stay a trial, I can drive to sixty-five and train a few more crews.
S0.do: Keeps training drivers and attending union meetings as usual. Uses the AI program a bit more for paperwork and keeps saving about three hundred a fortnight with Pete.
S0.feel: Relieved, like a storm passing the pit without rain.
S0.quote: Those eight trucks in the north pit have been sitting in the back of my mind for a year.
S0.fieldNote: Amira has already lived next to automation, so even the calm picture reveals a background worry she hadn't voiced before. Her instinct is to turn the conversation to safety and fatigue, which she sees as the real daily risk. She is practical and steady rather than ideological in tone, though her loyalties are clearly with the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say if the trucks are going driverless, the company owes us retraining, and the government should make sure of it. Some of the best people in that control room should be former drivers. I'd say that at work and in the union newsletter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the haul truck is the first thing to go, everyone in mining knows that. Steady change for the country could be fast change for me. The question is whether a 58-year-old woman gets one of the control room jobs or whether they hire twenty-five-year-olds who grew up on game consoles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put my name down for the autonomous fleet controller course the day they announce it, and ask the union to make sure senior drivers get first go. I'd start using the AI tools more so I'm not lost when I get there, maybe an hour a week with Jonas. And I'd keep driving until the last manual truck is parked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can see it coming down the ramp at me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Kayla and the newer drivers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to get into the control room course now, while they're young, and not to wait for the company to ask. I'd probably feel like a hypocrite, because I'd be the one telling them to leave the job I'm training them for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes you think you'd be good in a control room?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know what every bump on that ramp does to a loaded truck, and the people in the city don't. When a driverless truck stops for no reason, I'd know if it's a puddle or a real problem. That has to be worth something, even if nobody's paid for it yet.

S1.say: If the trucks go driverless, the company owes us retraining and the government should make sure of it. Former drivers belong in that control room.
S1.think: The haul truck is the first thing to go, so steady change for the country could be fast change for me. I don't know if a 58-year-old woman gets a control room job or if they hire young gamers.
S1.do: Signs up for the autonomous fleet controller course as soon as it's offered and asks the union to give senior drivers first go. Practises with AI tools for an hour a week with her son and keeps driving until the last manual truck is parked.
S1.feel: Anxious, as if it's coming down the ramp at her.
S1.quote: I'd be the one telling them to leave the job I'm training them for.
S1.fieldNote: What looks mild for most workers lands hard on haul truck drivers, and Amira knows it. She plans to move rather than dig in, but she worries about age and gender bias in who gets the new control room jobs. The image of training people for a job she's urging them to leave clearly troubles her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need unions and a government that steps in. Somebody has to make the companies share what they save. I'd be on the picket line if it came to that, and I'd say so online too, which I never do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be sixty in 2028, and the control room jobs would be gone too if AI can run the whole fleet. Pete's tyre shop lives off the mine trucks, so we'd both lose work at once. Three months of savings doesn't stretch over five years to the pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the savings plan going to the holiday fund and put it all into the emergency account. I'd ask the company straight out what an early retirement package looks like, before they offer it on their terms. And I'd push the union to fight for a wage bridge to sixty-five for older workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake listening to the trucks I can't see anymore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd both lose work. Talk me through that.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the mine trucks go driverless, they still need tyres, but the company would buy them direct with a service contract, not from Pete. His shop has three staff who are all mates' kids. We'd be sitting at the kitchen table with two businesses' worth of bad news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell Ali to keep studying mining engineering?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd tell him to switch at the end of the semester. Maybe to something with people, like teaching or nursing, though I don't know if those are safe either. That's the bit that scares me most, I don't know what to tell him.

S2.say: This is exactly why we need unions and a government that steps in to make companies share what they save. I'd be on the picket line and saying so online.
S2.think: I'd be sixty, and the control room jobs would be gone too if AI runs the whole fleet. Pete's tyre shop depends on the mine, so we'd both lose work, and three months of savings won't stretch to the pension.
S2.do: Moves all savings into an emergency fund and asks the company what an early retirement package looks like before they set the terms. Pushes the union to fight for a wage bridge to sixty-five and tells her son to switch out of mining engineering.
S2.quote: I'd be lying awake listening to the trucks I can't see anymore.
S2.fieldNote: The fast scenario hits Amira twice because her husband's business depends on the same mine. Her steady, wait-for-proof approach has no time to work here, and she knows the control room escape route closes too. Her deepest worry is not knowing what career to recommend to her son.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to do this properly if the government gets moving now. Retraining money, a levy on the companies that automate, and protection for older workers. I'd be saying it at the union and writing to our local member.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, 2031 puts me at sixty-three. If I can get into the control room by 2028, I'd probably last until the AI takes that over too, and by then I'm close to done. It's tight, but I can see a path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the fleet controller course in the first year and move into the control room by the second. Pete and I would push our savings from three months to six by putting the holiday money in. And I'd tell Ali to finish his degree but add a teaching certificate on the side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's the kind I can work with. I'd have a checklist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is this different from the 2028 one for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is a crash. Five years is a hard landing, but you see the runway. It's the difference between being tipped out of the truck and being told to park it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Pete's shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd have time to start doing car and farm tyres, not just mine work. He's already got a mate with a farm supply business out on the highway. It wouldn't replace the mine money, but it would keep the doors open.

S3.say: Five years is enough to do this properly if the government gets moving now, with retraining money, a levy on companies that automate, and protection for older workers.
S3.think: I'd be sixty-three in 2031. If I get into the control room by 2028, I'd probably last until AI takes that over too, and by then I'm nearly done, so it's tight but there's a path.
S3.do: Takes the fleet controller course in year one and moves into the control room by year two. Builds savings from three to six months and asks her son to add a teaching certificate to his degree.
S3.feel: Anxious, but in a way she can manage with a plan.
S3.quote: It's the difference between being tipped out of the truck and being told to park it.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Amira's steady style suddenly works for her: she can wait for the control room to be proven and still get in. She separates the national picture, which she wants government to manage, from her own narrow path. Pete's shop becomes a second thread of planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and if we waste it, that's on the politicians and the boards. It's enough time to retrain a whole town. I'd be pushing for a proper transition plan in the next two agreements.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me personally, I'd likely retire in 2033 before it fully arrives. I'd spend my last years in the control room or training the people who run the robots. It's the younger crews I'd be thinking about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving for now and move to the control room when the north pit trial goes site-wide, probably in four or five years. I'd keep our savings plan going and pay off the last bit of the car loan. Through the union, I'd push for a training fund for under-forties paid by an automation levy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy for the town, but mostly okay for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're okay for yourself, but uneasy for the town. What does the town lose?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pete's shop, the café on the main street, the junior football team, because families leave when the jobs go. I've seen it happen at the old nickel town up the road. It took about five years for the school to halve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your boys in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jonas has time to move from mine electrics into something like solar farms or the grid. Ali has time to finish and pick a direction that's still around in 2036, whatever that is. I'd tell them both what my mum told me: learn the thing nobody else wants to learn.

S4.say: Ten years is a gift, and if we waste it, that's on the politicians and the boards. It's enough time to retrain a whole town.
S4.think: I'd probably retire in 2033 before it fully arrives, after a few years in the control room or training the people who run the robots. It's the younger crews I'd be thinking about.
S4.do: Keeps driving for now and moves to the control room when the driverless trial goes site-wide in four or five years. Keeps the savings plan, pays off the car loan, and pushes through the union for a training fund paid by an automation levy.
S4.feel: Mostly okay for herself, a little uneasy for the town.
S4.quote: I'd tell them both what my mum told me: learn the thing nobody else wants to learn.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Amira's steady approach shine: she waits until the driverless fleet is proven, then moves. Her worry turns to the town, drawing on what she saw happen in a nearby nickel town. She keeps coming back to her sons, which seems to be her real measure of how bad a scenario is.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because it takes my job and Pete's shop in the same year, before we've saved enough. What would help is a guaranteed income to sixty-five for older workers who lose their jobs to automation, and some honest advice for my boys about which careers will still exist.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about women in mining. It took me fifteen years to be taken seriously in a haul truck, and I'm one of three women trainers on the whole site. I'd hate for all that to get wiped out before the next lot of women even get a turn.

headlineQuote: It took me fifteen years to be taken seriously in a haul truck, and I'm one of three women trainers on the whole site.
portrait: Amira Jensen is a 58-year-old haul truck driver and lead trainer at an open-pit iron ore mine, where driverless trucks are already on trial in the next pit. She's union-minded and practical, uses AI now and then for paperwork, and moves once something is proven. Because haul trucks are first in line for automation, she is anxious even in the steady scenario, and alarmed by AGI in two years, when her job and her husband's tyre shop could go together. With five or ten years she sees a path through the control room to retirement and turns her worry to her sons and the town.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it would take both her job and her husband's tyre shop before they have enough saved.
whatWouldHelp: A guaranteed income to sixty-five for older workers displaced by automation, plus honest career advice for her sons.
